summary: Sirach 47 continues the praise of Israel’s ancestors by moving from Nathan to David, celebrating David’s courage, victories, worship, and covenantal throne. It then turns to Solomon, praising his peace, wisdom, fame, wealth, and temple-building before naming his folly and the division that followed. The chapter closes with mercy preserving David’s line while Rehoboam, Jeroboam, and Ephraim’s sin lead toward removal from the land.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Sirach remembers kings: greatness includes courage, wisdom, worship, and divine gifts, but failure has public consequences. It also keeps the book’s ancestor praise from becoming simple hero worship, because David and Solomon are praised within a story that includes sin, mercy, division, and judgment.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Originally students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, ancestral writings, and scribal instruction central to Ben Sira’s world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction and praise of ancestors, using poetic comparison, compact evaluation, and remembered history.

outline.heading: Nathan and David introduced
outline.note: Nathan appears in David’s days, and David is set apart from Israel by comparison with the fat of a peace offering.

outline.heading: David’s courage and victories
outline.note: David is remembered for facing lions, bears, Goliath, and surrounding enemies, with strength given by the Most High Lord.

outline.heading: David’s worship and covenant
outline.note: David gives thanks, orders singers and feast praise, and receives forgiveness, exaltation, and a covenant of kings.

outline.heading: Solomon’s peace, wisdom, and fame
outline.note: Solomon rises after David, rules in peace, builds a house for God’s name, and becomes renowned for wisdom, sayings, songs, and wealth.

outline.heading: Solomon’s folly and the divided kingdom
outline.note: The chapter directly blames Solomon’s subjection to women and folly for dishonor, grief, and the divided sovereignty.

outline.heading: Mercy, revolt, and exile
outline.note: God’s mercy preserves a remnant and a Davidic root, but Rehoboam, Jeroboam, and Ephraim’s multiplied sins move toward removal from the land.

keyVerses.text: In every work of his he gave thanks to the Holy One Most High with words of glory. He sang praise with his whole heart, and loved him who made him.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the chapter’s positive portrait of David around worship, gratitude, and love for his maker.

keyVerses.text: The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn forever. He gave him a covenant of kings, and a glorious throne in Israel.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the chapter’s account of David as forgiven, exalted, and linked to an enduring royal promise.

keyVerses.text: Solomon reigned in days of peace. God gave him rest all around, that he might set up a house for his name, and prepare a sanctuary forever.
keyVerses.why: This states the peaceful setting and temple purpose that shape the chapter’s praise of Solomon.

keyVerses.text: But the Lord will never forsake his mercy. He won’t destroy any of his works, nor blot out the posterity of his elect. He won’t take away the offspring of him who loved him. He gave a remnant to Jacob, and to David a root from his own family.
keyVerses.why: After Solomon’s failure and the kingdom’s division, this verse holds together judgment and continuing mercy.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with Nathan before David?
questions.answer: Verse 1 places Nathan in David’s days before the chapter’s main praise of David begins. The chapter does not retell Nathan’s actions in detail; it simply links prophetic witness with David’s reign before moving to David’s set-apart status and deeds.

questions.question: What does it mean that David was like the fat separated from the peace offering?
questions.answer: Verse 2 uses a worship image: the fat is singled out from the peace offering. The comparison presents David as specially set apart from the children of Israel and introduces the praise of his deeds.

questions.question: How does the chapter describe David’s early courage?
questions.answer: Verses 3-4 picture David as facing dangerous animals and defeating Goliath in his youth. The chapter emphasizes that the victory took away reproach from the people and beat down Goliath’s boasting. Verse 5 adds that David called on the Most High Lord and received strength for the act.

questions.question: What is meant by the repeated image of a horn?
questions.answer: In this chapter, horn is an image of strength, honor, or power. David’s victory is said to exalt the horn of his people, the Philistines’ horn is broken, and David’s own horn is exalted forever. The image helps connect military deliverance, public honor, and royal standing.

questions.question: Why is David praised for singers, feasts, and the sanctuary?
questions.answer: Verses 8-10 present David as a worshiping king who gives thanks, sings praise, appoints singers, and orders festal praise so that the sanctuary resounds. The chapter’s interest is not only in David’s battles but also in worship arranged with beauty and regularity.

questions.question: Does the chapter ignore David’s sins?
questions.answer: No. Verse 11 says, “The Lord took away his sins,” which means the chapter knows David had sins even while praising him. It does not narrate those sins here; it emphasizes forgiveness, exaltation, and the covenant of kings.

questions.question: How does Sirach portray Solomon before criticizing him?
questions.answer: Verses 12-18 first praise Solomon as David’s wise son who lived in security, reigned in peace, built a house for God’s name, and became famous for understanding, parables, riddles, songs, proverbs, and wealth. The criticism comes only after that large positive portrait, so the chapter asks readers to hold both Solomon’s gifts and failures together.

questions.question: How should readers handle the statement that Solomon bowed his loins to women?
questions.answer: Verse 19 places Solomon’s submission to women within the account of his downfall. Verses 20–21 address him directly for folly that damaged his honor and descendants and led to divided rule. The accusation reflects an ancient male perspective suspicious of women, but its stated target is Solomon’s failure; it is not evidence that women as a group cause men’s wrongdoing.

questions.question: What hope remains after the kingdom is divided?
questions.answer: Verse 22 says the Lord will not forsake mercy, destroy his works, or blot out the posterity of his elect. The chapter names a remnant for Jacob and a root from David’s family, even as verses 23-25 describe foolish rule, Israel’s sin, and removal from the land. Hope is present, but it is not used to erase the seriousness of the chapter’s judgment.

glossary.def: A prophet named at the start of the chapter as rising up to prophesy in David’s days.
A sacrificial offering used in verse 2 as the comparison for David being separated from the children of Israel.
The boasting giant whom David is said to have beaten down with a sling stone.
The title used in verse 5 for the one David called upon for strength.
The holy place associated in this chapter with ordered praise under David and with Solomon’s building purpose.
The surviving people God gives to Jacob after the chapter has described sin, division, and judgment.
